cf.title: Let's drop support for named POSIX semaphores

input.subject: Let's drop support for named POSIX semaphores

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The proposal states the problem and the change, removes an untested path that meson cannot select, and leaves SysV and unnamed POSIX semaphores in place. The one open point is whether an out-of-tree configure build still selects named semaphores; the material shows none.

brief.title: Drop support for named POSIX semaphores (sem_open)
brief.problem: Postgres keeps a sem_open() semaphore implementation that no platform prefers and that nobody tests. macOS, the original reason for it, has used SysV semaphores for a long time, and the meson build offers no way to select it.
brief.proposed_design: The patch removes the named POSIX semaphore path from posix_sema.c and the configure, meson and darwin template logic that can select it. SysV semaphores and unnamed POSIX semaphores (sem_init) stay as the two supported implementations.
user_visible_surface: The configure-time choice of named POSIX semaphores (USE_NAMED_POSIX_SEMAPHORES in pg_config.h.in) goes away.
author_claims: Named POSIX semaphores do not work with EXEC_BACKEND.
They typically use a file descriptor or similar resource per semaphore per backend, so the cost grows as N squared for N backends.
No platform prefers them, and the OpenBSD tests showed poor performance that any platform would share because of the POSIX API.
The code is long untested, and meson cannot select it today.
brief.thread_state: Shihao Zhong, Heikki Linnakangas and Greg Burd support it, and Peter Eisentraut withdrew his concern about adding a SysV dependency for macOS sandboxing. The discussion moved to a futex-based replacement for semaphores, and Tom plans follow-up fixes for the unused IPCProtection macro, runtime.sgml and comments.
unclear: The material has no v2 patch with Shihao's cleanup and the runtime.sgml fix.
The proposal does not say whether any packager or out-of-tree build still selects named semaphores with configure.
The commit message does not say whether the release notes will mention the removal.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch removes USE_NAMED_POSIX_SEMAPHORES from pg_config.h.in, a macro that out-of-tree code could test.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch deletes a semaphore path in posix_sema.c and its configure, meson and darwin template logic, which lowers the burden.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Does any packager or out-of-tree build still select named POSIX semaphores through configure, for example by setting USE_NAMED_POSIX_SEMAPHORES?
Will the release notes mention the removal so that anyone who builds with named semaphores learns of it?
Will a v2 include the cleanup from message #2: the unused IPCProtection macro, the unneeded includes, and the runtime.sgml sentence?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane, a committer, wrote the patch, and Heikki Linnakangas supported it in message #3. The owner needs to know the port-level semaphore code and the configure and meson build logic.
committability.liability: The owner signs for build breakage on any platform or out-of-tree build that still selected sem_open(). The risk is small and shows up at build time, soon after commit.
committability.author_follow_up: The thread state says the author plans follow-up fixes for the IPCProtection macro, runtime.sgml and comments.

priority.reason: The patch is small, touches six files, and only removes code that nobody tests and meson cannot select. A committer wrote it, three people support it, and the one concern raised in the thread was withdrawn.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so this review cannot confirm that the configure and darwin template changes leave SysV and unnamed POSIX selection unchanged on every platform. Only 3 of 11 messages were shown.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: I thought it would be better to add a POSIx_fadvise description for the recovery_prefetch parameter here, to distinguish it from the database functions.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The entry proposes adding a description of posix_fadvise to the documentation of the recovery_prefetch parameter, to set it apart from database functions. It is attached to the WAL prefetch thread, where recovery reads ahead in the WAL and calls PrefetchBuffer() for referenced blocks, which relies on POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. None of the shown messages discusses the documentation change. The last messages cover a buildfarm failure on topminnow, which Thomas Munro traced to pg_walinspect rather than to the prefetch code.

precedents_retrieved.title: [PROPOSAL] : Disallow use of empty column name in (column_name '') in ALTER or CREATE of foreign table.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes postgres_fdw's validator reject empty values for the column_name, schema_name and table_name options in create or alter foreign table. Today an empty column_name is accepted, and the remote query then fails with a zero-length identifier error.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane judged that the check did not add enough ease-of-use to justify the extra code, and he compared an empty name to a misspelled remote name, which cannot be checked either. Robert Haas pointed out that existing foreign tables with empty values would then fail pg_dump or pg_upgrade. Nobody argued for the patch after Tom voted against it, so Robert marked it Rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I was down on it to start with, on the grounds that it wasn't adding enough ease-of-use to justify even a relatively small amount of added code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Named Operators
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Matthias van de Meent, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets users name operators as identifiers between colons, such as :distance: or :contains_all:, and use them infix in queries in place of symbol operators like <#>. The scanner keeps the colons in the stored operator name, and the grammar does not change.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Matthias van de Meent objected that :name: shadows common variable substitution patterns, including those of psql, and that users could call the underlying function directly. Tom Lane judged that no concise syntax would be safe from future SQL spec extensions, and that "a {foo} b" offers nothing over "foo(a,b)". He proposed teaching the planner to optimize function calls like their operators instead. No updated patch followed, so Daniel Gustafsson returned it with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There seems very little chance that we can invent a syntax that
is concise, non-ugly, and not likely to get blindsided by future
SQL spec extensions.

precedents_retrieved.title: some namespace.c refactoring
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patches replace the repetitive per-object "is visible" and get_*_oid() functions in namespace.c with common code that uses objectaddress.c lookups for the syscache and attribute numbers of each catalog. Functions with special behavior were left unchanged.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane doubted that the patch preserves existing semantics and expected a performance penalty, and Alvaro Herrera pointed to the linear scan in get_object_property_data(). The author's own benchmark showed the "is visible" functions about 2 times slower in a tight loop, and his attempts to speed up get_object_property_data() helped little. Tom Lane did not answer the question about semantics in the visible messages. After almost a year without activity, vignesh C closed the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I have
very serious concerns first about whether it even preserves the
existing semantics, and second about whether there is a performance
penalty.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Fix bogus %name-prefix option syntax in all our Bison files."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Fix bogus %name-prefix option syntax in all our Bison files."
Reverted commit(s): Fix bogus %name-prefix option syntax in all our Bison files.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 45b7abe59e9485657ac9380f35d2d917dd0da25b.

It turns out that the %name-prefix syntax without "=" does not work
at all in pre-2.4 Bison.  We are not prepared to make such a large
jump in minimum required Bison version just to suppress a warning
message in a version hardly any developers are using yet.
When 3.0 gets more popular, we'll figure out a way to deal with this.
In the meantime, BISONFLAGS=-Wno-deprecated is recommendable for
anyone using 3.0 who doesn't want to see the warning.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memoize ANTI and SEMI JOIN inner
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner put a Memoize node on the parameterized inner side of a Nested Loop semi join or anti join, so pulled-up EXISTS and NOT EXISTS sublinks can reuse cached inner results. It relies on Memoize single-row mode, because each outer row needs only the first inner match.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Richard Guo showed that the change is unsafe for semi and anti joins unless the inner side is provably unique. Join clauses from an upper level can move to the semi join, so a second inner tuple arrives and fails with "cache entry already complete". A semi join with a provably unique inner is already reduced to an inner join, so the work narrowed to proving inner_unique for anti joins, and Richard Guo posted a patch for that. The visible messages do not show why the entry was then withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I conducted some experiments, and I'm afraid it's not safe to consider Memoize for semi or anti joins, unless the inner side is provably unique.

precedents_retrieved.title: rand48 replacement
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the rand48 generator with a new pg_prng module based on xoroshiro128**, using a 128-bit state, and use it for all internal random number needs. The module hides the algorithm behind an interface and changes pgbench to use portable integer code instead of code that relies on doubles.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. No one objected: Tomas Vondra asked for the motivation, and Aleksander Alekseev reviewed the patch, posted a v2 and marked the tests as passing. Aleksander Alekseev also apologized for a duplicate commitfest entry, which may explain a same-day withdrawal, but the text does not say which entry was withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use AF_UNIX for tests on Windows (ie drop fallback TCP code)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Thomas Munro proposed using AF_UNIX sockets for pg_regress and TAP tests on Windows too, removing the Windows-only TCP and SSPI setup code in the test harness. To match Unix security, mkdtemp() on Windows would create the socket directory with access for the current user only.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that with TCP gone from the Windows tests, the TCP socket code would have little test coverage on any platform, and reviewers asked for a switch that runs the tests over either TCP or Unix sockets. The author agreed, set the TAP test patch aside for more work and posted only the first two patches. Those later stopped applying, the author posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If we remove that, won't we have a whole lot of code that's not
tested at all on any platform, ie all the TCP-socket code?

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Allow --with-bonjour to work with non-macOS implementations of Bonjour."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Allow --with-bonjour to work with non-macOS implementations of Bonjour."
Reverted commit(s): Allow --with-bonjour to work with non-macOS implementations of Bonjour.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Upon further review, our Bonjour code doesn't actually work with the
Avahi not-too-compatible compatibility library.  While you can get it
to work on non-macOS platforms if you link to Apple's own mDNSResponder
code, there don't seem to be many people who care about that.  Leaving in
the AC_SEARCH_LIBS call seems more likely to encourage people to build
broken configurations than to do anything very useful.

Hence, remove the AC_SEARCH_LIBS call and put in a warning comment instead.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Change SHA2 implementation based on OpenSSL to use EVP digest routines"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Change SHA2 implementation based on OpenSSL to use EVP digest routines"
Reverted commit(s): Change SHA2 implementation based on OpenSSL to use EVP digest routines
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit e21cbb4, as the switch to EVP routines requires a
more careful design where we would need to have at least our wrapper
routines return a status instead of issuing an error by themselves to
let the caller do the error handling.  The memory handling was also
incorrect and could cause leaks in the backend if a failure happened,
requiring most likely a callback to do the necessary cleanup as the only
clean way to be able to allocate an EVP context requires the use of an
allocation within OpenSSL.  The potential rework of the wrappers also
impacts the fallback implementation when not building with OpenSSL.

Originally, prairiedog has reported a compilation failure, but after
discussion with Tom Lane this needs a better design.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found that proposed or rejected removing named POSIX semaphores. [P10] reverted removal of a macOS readline workaround because macOS still ships old libedit; here macOS has preferred SysV semaphores since 2002 and meson cannot select named semaphores, so that reason does not apply. [P5] supports the removal, since one-FD-per-semaphore platforms broke a test. Message #1 cites an OpenBSD discussion that found named semaphores perform poorly and did not proceed.

The only user-facing contract is the configure-time selection of named semaphores. The meson build already cannot select it, and macOS has defaulted to SysV for years, so no build, script or default behaviour should change. No SQL, GUC, catalog, pg_dump or psql surface is touched. [P10] reverted a macOS-related removal, but its reason was an old libedit still shipped in the base system, and the proposal names no platform that still relies on sem_open(). A release-note line for packagers is a small follow-up, not an objection.

The patch changes no persistent or cross-node state: no on-disk format, WAL, catalog, protocol or replication change. Named semaphores live only while the server runs, and removing the pg_config.h macro is a major-release build change with no stated extension ABI impact. Platform portability, such as [P10], belongs to other angles.

The patch removes a build-time semaphore option and adds no privilege, exposure or authentication surface. If anything, it removes named semaphores that live in a system-wide namespace, which shrinks the exposure. The remaining SysV and unnamed POSIX paths are unchanged, so no security or privilege objection applies.

The patch removes code, so long-run maintenance cost goes down: one fewer configure branch and one fewer path in posix_sema.c that nobody tests and meson cannot build. It adds nothing on any hot path, and it reverts the darwin template only where it already prefers SysV semaphores. The patch author is a committer who knows the area, and Heikki Linnakangas also supports it. The only remaining concern is the macOS sandboxing direction, which Peter Eisentraut withdrew in message #11. The one leftover risk is an out-of-tree build that sets USE_NAMED_POSIX_SEMAPHORES through configure, but the material shows no such user. [P10], a macOS-related removal that was later reverted, involved a library macOS still ships, so its reason does not apply here.

This angle does not apply to a removal. The proposal deletes a second sem_open() path while SysV and unnamed POSIX semaphores stay, which reduces duplicated mechanisms. No extension or existing feature competes with it, and the futex direction discussed in messages #5, #8 and #10 is a separate future proposal.

The proposal removes code and adds no feature, so the demand question applies to the code being removed. The material shows no current user of named POSIX semaphores. macOS has preferred SysV semaphores since 2002, meson cannot select the named kind, and the OpenBSD discussion in message #1 ended on poor performance. Four people supported the removal in the thread, and Peter Eisentraut withdrew his concern in message #11. [P10] was a removal reverted because of an old macOS libedit, but that reason does not apply here because macOS has had SysV semaphores for decades. The material cannot show whether any out-of-tree configure build still selects USE_NAMED_POSIX_SEMAPHORES; a release-note mention would cover that case.
